topic.examWeightHint: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. A tree diagram is a whole question of 5 to 8 marks: Summer 2025 Q7 ran complete the tree [2], a two-branch probability [3], a conditional [3]; Summer 2024 Q3 ran a single write-down [1], then 2- and 2-mark reads, then a conditional part [3]; Summer 2026 Q4 opened with a one-mark completion. The command words are Complete, Calculate and Write down. Marks go to a branch product written down (MW1), then to the sum of the qualifying branches (W1). Exact fractions are expected, and follow-through applies from a candidate's own tree.

sheet.howExamined: Unit 3 is one 1-hour calculator paper of 50 marks, sat every Summer. A tree diagram is a whole question of 5 to 8 marks: Summer 2025 Q7 ran complete the tree [2], a two-branch probability [3], a conditional [3]; Summer 2024 Q3 ran a single write-down [1], then 2- and 2-mark reads, then a conditional part [3]; Summer 2026 Q4 opened with a one-mark completion. The command words are Complete, Calculate and Write down. Marks go to a branch product written down (MW1), then to the sum of the qualifying branches (W1). Exact fractions are expected, and follow-through applies from a candidate's own tree.
traps: Multiplying two same-colour branch results instead of adding them, and losing accuracy by switching to rounded decimals part-way through (Summer 2019 FM3 Q2)
Adding two probabilities where the question asks for both events together: examiners called this a straightforward opener that many got wrong (Summer 2022 FM3 Q1)
Counting one order only for 'one of each', which halves the answer (Summer 2022 FM3 Q6)
Working with replacement throughout when the items are kept, so the second and third denominators never drop (Summer 2024 FM3 Q3)
Adding every qualifying branch instead of taking the other result from 1: for 'different colours' that meant six products where one subtraction would do, and slips followed (Summer 2024 FM3 Q3)

Drawing the tree is rarely where the marks go: almost every candidate completed it correctly, and the marks were lost later, in the conditional part that divides one branch product by a sum of branches (Summer 2025 FM3 Q7)

steps.decision: Nothing has been taken yet, so both denominators are 8. Writing the first stage down before the second keeps the two apart.

steps.decision: One counter has gone, so every second denominator is 7. Only the colour already taken loses one from its numerator.

options: 7, because one counter has been taken and not put back
8, because the bag is the same bag
6, because two counters are being taken altogether
whyMenu.explain: The second draw happens after one counter has left. Keeping 8 would give $0.31$ for two reds instead of $0.36$.

steps.working: Red then white: $\dfrac{5}{8} \times \dfrac{3}{7} = \dfrac{15}{56}$. White then red: $\dfrac{3}{8} \times \dfrac{5}{7} = \dfrac{15}{56}$.
steps.decision: Multiply along each branch. Two different colours can come out in either order, so both branches belong to the event.

steps.decision: Find the second branch of each pair by subtracting from 1. The two branches leaving a point always total 1, which is the quickest check on a tree.

steps.working: The seeds are independent, so the second stage carries the same two probabilities as the first.
steps.decision: Independent means the first outcome changes nothing. That is what makes this different from a without-replacement tree, where the second stage has to be recalculated.

steps.working: Grows then fails: $0.8 \times 0.2 = 0.16$. Fails then grows: $0.2 \times 0.8 = 0.16$.
steps.decision: Exactly one is two different paths, not one. Writing both down before adding is what stops the answer being halved.
Add the two branches. A check: the four paths come to 0.64 + 0.32 + 0.04 = 1.

twin.stem: With the same two seeds, calculate the probability that at least one of them grows.

items.stem: Before the lesson, a check on something you already know. What is $\dfrac{2}{5} \times \dfrac{3}{4}$, in its simplest form?

options.feedback: Yes: $\dfrac{6}{20}$, which cancels by 2. Every branch of a tree is a product like this.
The numerators and the denominators have been added separately. Multiplying fractions multiplies top by top and bottom by bottom.
The two fractions have been crossed over. Multiply straight across: $2 \times 3$ over $5 \times 4$.

items.stem: Another check on earlier work. What is $\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{1}{3}$?
items.skill: Adding fractions with different denominators (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: $\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{3}{6}$. Adding branch results needs a common denominator.
The numerators and denominators have been added separately, which is not how fractions add. Rewrite both over 6 first.
That is the product, not the sum. Adding needs a common denominator.

items.stem: One more from earlier work, before anything new. A bag holds 7 red and 3 green beads. One bead is taken and kept. How many beads are left in the bag?
items.skill: Tracking a total after one item is removed (from GCSE Mathematics)

options.feedback: Yes: one of the 10 has gone. Without replacement, that 9 becomes the next denominator.
The bead was kept, not put back, so the bag is one smaller.
Only one bead has been taken, so the total drops by one, not two.

items.stem: A bag holds 4 lemon and 6 lime sweets. One is eaten, then another is taken. What is the probability that the second is lemon, given the first was lemon?

options.feedback: Yes: one lemon has gone, so 3 lemon are left among 9 sweets.
The total dropped but the lemon count did not. The sweet eaten was lemon, so the numerator falls too.
That is the probability for the first sweet, or for a sweet put back. One sweet has gone, so the denominator is 9.

items.stem: On a tree, $P(\text{A then B}) = 0.3$ and $P(\text{B then A}) = 0.3$. What is the probability of one A and one B, in either order?

options.feedback: Yes: the two branches are separate ways for the same event, so they add.
Only one order has been counted, which halves the answer. Examiners reported this exact slip in 2022.
The two branch results have been multiplied. Multiplying would ask for both orders at once, which cannot happen.

items.stem: On a two-stage tree, one path gives $P = \dfrac{1}{6}$ and another gives $P = \dfrac{1}{3}$. The event happens on either path. What is its probability?
items.skill: Adding across branches rather than multiplying

options.feedback: Yes: two separate branches add. $\dfrac{1}{6} + \dfrac{2}{6} = \dfrac{1}{2}$.
Multiplying asks for both paths to happen together, and a pair of outcomes only travels one path.
Only one of the two paths has been counted. Both satisfy the event, so both are added.

items.stem: $P(\text{no sixes in three rolls}) = 0.579$. What is $P(\text{at least one six in three rolls})$, to 3 decimal places?
items.skill: Using the complement for 'at least one'

options.feedback: Yes: $1 - 0.579$. 'At least one' is everything except 'none', which is one line rather than seven branches.
That is the probability of no sixes at all, which is the opposite event. Take it from 1.
The complement has been added to 1 rather than subtracted from it, and a probability is never above 1.

items.stem: Two events happen one after the other and both must occur. What do you do with the two branch probabilities?

options.feedback: Yes: along a branch every stage has to happen, so the probabilities multiply.
Adding is for separate branches that cannot both happen. Examiners reported this swap on a straightforward opening question in 2022.

options.text: Add them, then take off their product
options.feedback: That is the addition rule, which gives the probability that at least one of the two happens. Along a branch both must happen, so the probabilities multiply.

items.stem: Three counters are taken from a bag of 8 without replacement. What are the three denominators on the top path of the tree?
items.skill: Denominators on a three-stage without-replacement tree

options.feedback: Yes: one counter leaves the bag at each draw.
That is the with-replacement tree. Here the counters are kept, so the bag shrinks.
The third draw follows two removals, so the denominator has dropped twice.

Complete the tree diagram by choosing the probability for each of the branches (i) to (iv).

the two branches after a black pen: 7/10 and 3/10

parts.workedSolution:
After a blue pen: 6 blue and 4 black among 10, so (i) is 6/10 and (ii) is 4/10.
After a black pen: 7 blue and 3 black among 10, so (iii) is 7/10 and (iv) is 3/10.

parts.stem: Using the tree diagram, calculate the probability that both pens taken are blue.
hints: Follow the top path of the tree.
The second denominator is 10.

commonErrors.feedback: That is $\dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{7}{11}$, the answer if the first pen had been put back. Without replacement the case holds 10 pens, 6 of them blue, for the second draw: $\dfrac{7}{11} \times \dfrac{6}{10} = \dfrac{21}{55}$.
The two branch probabilities have been added. Along a branch both things have to happen, so they multiply: $\dfrac{21}{55}$. Adding also gives an answer above 1, which no probability can be.

context.setting: Three pens taken from a pencil case without replacement

parts.stem:
A pencil case holds 11 pens: 7 blue and 4 black. Three pens are taken out one after the other, without replacement.
The first two pens taken are blue.
Write down the probability that the third pen is also blue.
hints: Two blue pens have already gone.
Two pens have gone altogether, so 9 are left.
parts.workedSolution: 5 blue pens are left among 9, so the probability is $\dfrac{5}{9}$.

parts.stem: Calculate the probability that all three pens taken are blue.
hints: Follow the top path of the three-stage tree.
The denominators are 11, 10 and 9.

commonErrors.feedback: Every stage has been worked as if the pen before it went back, so it is still 7 blue out of 11 each time. Without replacement the pens fall to 10 and then 9, and the blue ones with them, giving $\dfrac{7}{33}$.
The three branch probabilities have been added, which gives a number above 1. Along a path every stage must happen, so they multiply: $\dfrac{7}{33}$.

parts.stem: Calculate the probability that at least one of the three pens taken is black.
hints: Only one of the eight paths has no black pen at all.
Take part (b) from 1.
parts.workedSolution:
The only path with no black pen is blue, blue, blue, which is $\dfrac{7}{33}$.
$P(\text{at least one black}) = 1 - \dfrac{7}{33} = \dfrac{26}{33}$.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability that all three are blue, which is the opposite event. 'At least one black' is everything else: $1 - \dfrac{7}{33} = \dfrac{26}{33}$.

questions.solutionProgram: third blue = 5/9; all blue = 7/11 * 6/10 * 5/9 = 7/33; at least one black = 1 - 7/33 = 26/33

context.setting: Three socks taken from a drawer in the dark

parts.stem:
A drawer holds 8 socks: 5 black and 3 grey. In the dark, three socks are taken out one after the other, without replacement.
Calculate the probability that all three socks are black.
hints: Multiply along the all-black path.
The denominators are 8, 7 and 6.

commonErrors.feedback: Every draw has been worked as if the sock went back, so it is still 5 black out of 8 each time. Kept socks leave the drawer: 8, then 7, then 6, giving $\dfrac{5}{28}$.
The three branch probabilities have been added, which gives more than 1. Along a path every draw must happen, so they multiply: $\dfrac{5}{28}$.

parts.stem: Calculate the probability that all three socks are the same colour.
hints: All black or all grey: two paths.
Separate paths add.
parts.workedSolution:
All grey is $\dfrac{3}{8} \times \dfrac{2}{7} \times \dfrac{1}{6}$, which is $\dfrac{1}{56}$.
$P(\text{same}) = \dfrac{5}{28} + \dfrac{1}{56}$, which is $\dfrac{11}{56}$.

commonErrors.feedback: The all-black and all-grey results have been multiplied. Three socks travel one path only, so the two paths add: $\dfrac{11}{56}$.
Both paths have been worked as if every sock went back. Kept, the denominators fall 8, 7, 6, and the answer is $\dfrac{11}{56}$.

parts.stem: Calculate the probability that the three socks are not all the same colour.
hints: Not all the same is everything except the two matching paths.
Take part (b) from 1.
parts.workedSolution: $1 - \dfrac{11}{56}$, which is $\dfrac{45}{56}$. Adding the six mixed paths gives the same, with six chances to slip.

commonErrors.feedback: That is the probability that all three match, the opposite event. 'Not all the same' is everything else: $1 - \dfrac{11}{56}$, which is $\dfrac{45}{56}$.

findTheMistake.stem: Conor was asked for the probability that two pens taken from a case of 11 (7 blue, 4 black), without replacement, are the same colour. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Lines 1 and 2 are both right, denominators and all. Line 3 multiplies them. Multiplying asks for both branches to happen at once, and a single pair of pens travels one branch only. Two separate branches add.
findTheMistake.feedback: Both branch products are correct, so the method mark and the working mark for them stand. The final mark is lost at line 3. A quick sense check would have caught it: 126/3025 is far smaller than either branch on its own, and adding two chances can never make the result smaller. The answer is $\dfrac{27}{55}$.

findTheMistake.stem: Declan was asked for the probability that two sweets taken from a bag of 10 (6 lemon, 4 orange), without replacement, are one of each flavour. His working:
findTheMistake.whatWentWrong: Line 1 is right. Line 2 stops at one order. Orange then lemon is just as much 'one of each', and its branch gives the same product, so both are added.
findTheMistake.feedback: His branch product is right, but the method mark is for both orders, so the marks go at line 2. A check would have caught it: the same-flavour paths come to 7/15, and with his 4/15 the four paths would not add to 1. The answer is $\dfrac{8}{15}$.

prompts.prompt: The two rules for reading a probability tree.
prompts.answer: Multiply along a branch, because every stage has to happen. Add across branches, because they are separate ways for the same event.

prompts.prompt: What changes on the second stage of a tree when there is no replacement?
prompts.answer: The denominator drops by one, and the numerator drops by one too on the branches where an item of that kind has already gone.

prompts.prompt: A question asks for one of each colour. Why is one branch product not enough?
prompts.answer: Either colour can come out first, so two branches satisfy the event and counting one of them halves the answer.

prompts.prompt: What is the quickest way to answer 'at least one', and why?
prompts.answer: Work out the probability of none and subtract it from 1, because none is a single branch while at least one is several.

prompts.prompt: Why should tree answers stay as exact fractions?
prompts.answer: Rounding to decimals part-way through loses accuracy, and marks have been lost that way; multiply the fractions and cancel at the end.

prompts.prompt: What do the two probabilities leaving one point of a tree always add to, and what is that useful for?
prompts.answer: They add to 1, which is the quickest check that a branch has been filled in correctly.

prompts.prompt: Three items are taken from ten without replacement. What are the three denominators?
prompts.answer: 10, then 9, then 8, because one item leaves at each draw.

findings.asked: Probability that two (then three) beads drawn without replacement are the same colour.
findings.wentWrong: Most understood a sum of pair products and of triple products, but a few multiplied P(BB) and P(GG) instead of adding them; some who switched to decimals lost accuracy through rounding.
findings.fullMarkAnswersDid: Multiplied along each branch, added the branches that satisfy the event, and kept every probability as an exact fraction.
findings.rule: Along a branch multiply; across mutually exclusive branches add; stay in fractions.

findings.asked: Probability that two independent events both happen.
findings.wentWrong: A straightforward opener that many got wrong: the two probabilities were identified and then added instead of multiplied (some even added numerators and denominators separately).
findings.rule: 'Both' or 'and' means multiply the probabilities; adding is only for 'either/or' of outcomes that cannot happen together.

findings.asked: Two students chosen, in either order, from a table of percentages.
findings.wentWrong: Only one order was counted, giving half the answer (0.014); this followed a conditional-probability part where the whole population was used as the denominator.
findings.rule: For 'one of each' count both orders: multiply along each branch, then add the two branches.

insight.ruleToRemember: Draw the tree, write the probability on every branch (denominators drop by one without replacement), multiply along a branch for 'and', add the qualifying branches for 'or', count both orders, and leave the answer as an exact fraction.
insight.aStarSignal: Setting up a without-replacement tree in one line and reading conditional probabilities straight off it - P(A given B) as the branch product over the probability of the condition.
